newsitem.title: INDIA: India steps up security for former Afghan leaders.
newsitem.headline: India steps up security for former Afghan leaders.

text.p: India stepped up security on Friday at the homes of former Afghan leaders in the capital New Delhi, police said.

Paramilitary troops surrounded a sprawling house in the exclusive Asian Games Village occupied by the widow of former Afghan president Najibullah, who was hanged by the Taleban militia after they took over the Afghan capital Kabul early on Friday.
The bodies of Najibullah and his brother Shahpur Ahmadzai were strung up from a concrete traffic-control post at the gates of the presidential palace as thousands crowded around to watch.
On Friday, soldiers took positions on neighbouring rooftops near Mrs Najibullah's home, who remained inside till noon. She then left in a bulletproof car.
The car took one of the main roads that lead to the airport, though it was not known if she headed there.
"She is aware of everything," an Indian police official, who supervised security arrangements at her home, told Reuters. "She is not well, it will be difficult for her to meet you."
The official said the home had been heavily guarded since Mrs Najibullah came to India more than four years ago with her three daughters.
Police were asked to step up security on Friday, he added.
Officials at the Afghan embassy in New Delhi said Mrs Najibullah had not approached them for help.
Security was also beefed up near the house of another former Afghan president, Babrak Karmal, about seven kilometres (four miles) away in another part of New Delhi.
"We heard the news on television, it's shocking," said Roman Baryalai, Karmal's nephew and a college student. "I am waiting for more news," he said.
He said he had not heard from his uncle, who was in Moscow.
An unknown number of wounded soldiers loyal to Afghan President Burhanuddin Rabbani are undergoing treatment in several private hospitals in the Indian capital.

Afghanistan's ambassador to India said Rabbani and other members of his government were about 25 km (15 miles) north of Kabul. He said the government still controlled 13 of Afghanistan's 31 provinces.
